strengths: The paper targets an important practical question: selecting or rejecting unsupervised pretext tasks before paying the cost of full SSL training would be useful if reliable.

The proposed decomposition into learnability, reliability, and completeness is an intuitive organizing lens that connects pretext-task fit, data validity of assumptions, and downstream-task alignment.
The empirical section attempts to test prediction of downstream performance across many augmentation-based pretext variants rather than reporting only one or two hand-picked tasks.
weaknesses: The central theory is not sound enough to support the claims. The key factorization of p(y|x) into learnability, reliability, and completeness terms is not justified as a valid probabilistic identity, and the subsequent error bounds appear to follow from definitions rather than proved assumptions. Several inequalities are asserted without clear conditions, independence assumptions, or proof.

The empirical estimators are circular or weak proxies for the proposed theoretical quantities. Reliability and completeness are estimated using a supervised target model trained on very few labels as an oracle substitute, so the method may mostly measure agreement with a noisy target classifier rather than true task relevance. It is unclear when such estimates would be reliable, especially in the low-label regime the paper emphasizes.

The experiments are too narrow for the broad claims. All tasks are simple CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 augmentation-strength variants under one model family and fixed hyperparameters; there are no realistic SSL methods beyond a simplified MSE consistency setup, no broader modalities, no stronger pretext tasks, and no evidence for neuro-symbolic settings despite the framing.

The evaluation reports only Pearson correlations and scatter plots, with no confidence intervals, repeated seeds, raw accuracy tables, rank-selection performance, comparisons to simple baselines such as small validation-set selection or augmentation severity heuristics, or ablations isolating the three proposed factors. A correlation around 0.7-0.8 may be useful, but the paper does not show that it leads to better task selection in practice.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript lacks code, seeds, implementation details for the alignment step, exact architectures/pretraining initialization, augmentation parameter handling, and full numerical results for the 115 tasks. The use of ViT-B for only 5 epochs on tiny labeled CIFAR subsets is also underspecified and unusual enough to require careful reporting.

Presentation has substantial issues: notation is often inconsistent or malformed, several claims are overstated as “rigorous theoretical analysis” despite missing proofs, figures are not quantitatively informative in the text, and references contain incomplete entries with “????”. There is also no meaningful limitations or ethics discussion.

strengths: The paper targets an important question: whether one can predict, before expensive training, which unsupervised pretext tasks will help downstream performance in semi/self-supervised learning.
The high-level decomposition into learnability, reliability, and completeness is intuitively appealing and could be a useful conceptual lens if formalized more carefully.

The empirical setup attempts to compare predicted and actual downstream performance over many pretext-task variants, and reports moderately high Pearson correlations on CIFAR-10/100 for both semi-supervised and self-supervised settings.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is not sound enough to support the paper's claims. Key quantities such as satisfaction of knowledge by f(x), y, or (x,K) are not rigorously defined, and the derivations are presented as inequalities without clear assumptions, proofs, or a well-specified probability space. Several steps read as informal intuition rather than theorem-level analysis.

The central bound is questionable. In the supposedly ideal reliable/complete case, the paper states R_target <= R_unlearnable, but if the pretext task is equivalent to the target task one would expect a much more carefully justified equality or equivalence under explicit assumptions. The later decomposition into unlearnable, unreliable, and incomplete terms appears constructed by partitioning errors, but this is not proven and the conditioning events are ambiguous.

The proposed empirical estimators are circular and fragile. Reliability and completeness are estimated using a target model trained on the scarce labeled data, so the method may partly measure the quality and biases of this small supervised model rather than intrinsic properties of the pretext task. This is especially problematic in the claimed low-label regime of only 5 examples per class.

The experiments are too narrow for the breadth of the claims. All validation is on CIFAR-10/100 with ViT-B and simple augmentation-based pretext tasks. The paper claims a broad unification of SSL and neuro-symbolic learning, but provides no experiments on genuine neuro-symbolic tasks, language tasks, structured reasoning, or modern SSL methods beyond augmentation consistency variants.

The evaluation reports only Pearson correlations and scatter plots. There are no confidence intervals, seeds, significance tests, calibration metrics, rank-selection accuracy, top-k task selection results, or comparisons to simple baselines such as validation on the few labeled samples, augmentation-strength heuristics, pretext loss alone, or supervised-proxy transferability measures.

Reproducibility is weak. Important details are missing or underspecified: exact training protocol for semi-supervised vs self-supervised learning, data splits, number of random seeds, initialization/pretraining status of ViT-B, augmentation composition, alignment procedure for f_pretext, and implementation details for computing the three indicators. No code or release plan is described.

Presentation quality is below the standard expected for ICML. The manuscript contains many grammatical issues, repeated phrasing, typos such as 'protext', references with missing years marked as '????', and figures/tables that are insufficiently explained. The related work is mostly descriptive and does not clearly position the contribution against prior theoretical work on SSL transferability or pretext-task alignment.

The limitations and ethics discussion are essentially absent. The paper does not discuss failure modes, dependence on the small supervised oracle, risks of misleading pretext-task selection, computational cost, or applicability boundaries. Given the strength of the claims, this omission is material.

Overall, the idea is potentially interesting, but the current manuscript has major technical, empirical, reproducibility, and presentation weaknesses. The evidence does not justify the claimed rigorous theory or broad practical usefulness, so I would recommend rejection.

strengths: The paper asks an important and timely question: how to estimate, before expensive training, whether an unsupervised pretext task will help a downstream target task. This is a practically useful problem for both semi-supervised and self-supervised learning.

The proposed decomposition into learnability, reliability, and completeness is conceptually appealing. It gives a useful vocabulary for discussing why pretext tasks help or hurt, and connects SSL pretext-task selection to neuro-symbolic ideas about imperfect prior knowledge.

The empirical section provides an encouraging initial signal: across 115 augmentation-based pretext tasks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the estimated score correlates reasonably with final semi-supervised and self-supervised performance, with reported Pearson correlations around 0.72-0.82.

The method is low-cost in spirit, using small labeled and unlabeled subsets to rank candidate pretext tasks. If validated more broadly, this could be useful for practitioners choosing augmentations or auxiliary objectives under limited labels.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are not yet soundly established. Equation (1) presents a factorization of p(y|x) through knowledge-satisfaction events, but the required probabilistic assumptions are not stated and the equality does not follow generally. Later generalization-error bounds appear closer to an intuitive error decomposition than a rigorous theorem, with no formal assumptions, proof details, or treatment of dependencies among the events.

The definitions of learnability, reliability, and completeness are not fully coherent for modern SSL settings. For example, f(x) is treated as both a target-task prediction and an object that can satisfy arbitrary pretext knowledge, while the alignment step for self-supervised representations is only sketched. This makes it hard to know exactly what is being measured beyond the specific augmentation-consistency experiments.

The empirical validation is too narrow for the breadth of the claims. All pretext tasks are simple image augmentations under a label-invariance assumption, evaluated only on CIFAR-10/100 with one architecture and one training recipe. This does not convincingly support claims about most SSL/Nesy scenarios, complex pretext tasks, NLP, larger-scale training, or general pretext-task selection.

The experiments report correlations but do not evaluate whether the proposed estimator actually improves task selection compared with cheaper or standard baselines, such as validation on a small labeled set, augmentation strength heuristics, pretext loss alone, linear-probe estimates, or individual components of the proposed score. There are also no confidence intervals, repeated runs, rank-correlation analyses, or statistical tests.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper gives high-level hyperparameters but omits many implementation details needed to reproduce the results, including exact training schedules, data splits/seeds, augmentation composition, how the three indicators are thresholded or computed from continuous losses, how target alignment is implemented, and whether code will be released.

Presentation needs polishing. Several claims are overstated, including 'rigorous theoretical analysis' and 'confirming the validity of the theory'; there are grammar issues, citation placeholders with missing years, and figures whose labels are small and cluttered. The limitations and ethical discussion are minimal; while the work has no obvious major ethical concern, it should discuss risks of selecting pretext tasks using a weak oracle trained from very few labels and possible dataset-specific biases.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: selecting useful SSL pretext tasks before paying the cost of full semi/self-supervised training and validation. A low-cost predictor for pretext-task utility would be valuable if reliable.
The framing in terms of learnability, reliability, and completeness is conceptually useful and gives a coherent vocabulary for why a pretext task may help or hurt a downstream target.

The empirical study has a nontrivial scale for a first pass: 115 augmentation-based pretext tasks, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-200, Office-31, ViT-B and ResNet-50, and checks with several standard SSL algorithms. The ablations suggest that reliability and completeness carry useful signal beyond learnability alone.

The method is concrete and relatively simple: fit a small pretext model, train a small supervised target surrogate, estimate assumption violations, and use prototype alignment for pretext embeddings. This makes the idea easy to understand and potentially inexpensive to apply.

The reported cost comparison is appealing: on CIFAR-10, estimation uses 50 labeled and 500 unlabeled samples and about 30 seconds versus full training/validation requiring far more data and around 1500-1650 seconds.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are not fully sound as stated. The derivation around Eq. 1 is not a justified probabilistic factorization of p(y|x), and the later inequalities are asserted with informal reasoning rather than proved under clear assumptions. The paper often treats the resulting expression as an estimator of actual target performance, but the derivation only resembles an upper-bound/error decomposition and does not establish calibration.

The empirical evidence mainly demonstrates Pearson correlation, not accurate quantitative estimation of target performance. The central claim says the method can estimate actual target performance, yet the evaluation does not report calibration error, ranking regret, top-k selection accuracy, confidence intervals across seeds, or comparisons to simple baselines such as small-validation-set selection, supervised-proxy accuracy alone, augmentation strength heuristics, or representation transferability metrics.

The experimental benchmark is narrow despite the large number of tasks. The 115 pretext tasks are mostly parameter sweeps of standard image augmentations under a label-invariance assumption, so the study does not convincingly cover richer SSL pretexts or non-vision settings. Some robustness results are only moderate or weak, e.g. correlations around 0.45-0.67 for several classic SSL algorithms and ResNet/model/OOD settings, which weakens the generality claim.

The estimator depends on a supervised model trained from the scarce labeled set and uses its pseudo-labels as an oracle for reliability and completeness. This creates a possible circularity: if the small supervised model is poor, biased, or benefits from the same augmentations, the estimates may reflect surrogate artifacts rather than true downstream performance. The paper does not analyze this failure mode or sensitivity to labeled-set sampling.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript gives datasets, model families, optimizer, learning rate, and batch size, but lacks code release, random seeds, exact data splits, details for all classic SSL implementations/hyperparameters, full numerical tables for all scatter plots, and variance over repeated runs. Many results appear to be single-run correlations.

Presentation needs substantial polishing. There are unresolved references to '??' in the appendix, grammatical errors, repeated sentences, and figures that are hard to inspect quantitatively. The paper also sometimes conflates accuracy/performance with error in notation, making the estimator harder to interpret.

The statistical testing is not very informative. Showing that correlations exceed a low critical value of 0.226 over 115 related pretext-task variants does not establish that the method accurately predicts performance, nor does it address dependence among augmentation strengths or multiple experimental conditions.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The impact statement is generic, and the paper does not seriously discuss when the estimator might fail, how misuse of pseudo-labels could affect sensitive domains, or the environmental cost of constructing the benchmark, although there are no obvious severe ethical concerns.

strengths: The paper targets a useful problem: estimating, before full SSL training and validation, whether an unsupervised pretext task is likely to help a downstream target task. This is practically relevant because pretext-task choice is often expensive and heuristic.

The framing around learnability, reliability, and completeness is potentially interesting, and the paper attempts to connect SSL pretext assumptions with broader knowledge-integrated learning concepts.

The experiments cover several datasets and settings, including CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-200, Office-31, multiple SSL algorithms, model backbones, data scales, and hyperparameters. The cost comparison also addresses an important practical motivation.
weaknesses: The central theory is not sound enough to support the claims. The factorization of p(y|x) into the proposed learnability/reliability/completeness terms is not justified, the event notation involving (x, KA) and (y, KA) is underspecified, and several inequalities appear asserted rather than derived. The resulting bound is too informal to serve as a rigorous generalization-error result.

The empirical estimators do not faithfully estimate the theoretical quantities. Reliability and completeness rely on a target model trained from only a few labels as a surrogate oracle, but the paper does not analyze or control the error of this surrogate. This can make the method circular: it estimates pretext usefulness largely through agreement with a weak supervised model.

The evaluation is much less convincing than claimed. The main metric is Pearson correlation across related augmentation strengths, not actual calibration, ranking quality, top-k selection success, or downstream regret. Some reported correlations are weak in important settings, e.g. about 0.45-0.67 for several self-supervised algorithms and 0.478 for ResNet semi-supervised learning, yet the paper still claims robust accurate prediction.

The benchmark of 115 pretext tasks is not as broad as advertised: it is mostly 11 standard augmentations swept over strengths. These points are highly dependent, so the hypothesis test treating all 115 as independent samples is inappropriate and overstates statistical evidence.

There are no strong baselines for the estimator, such as small-proxy training, augmentation-strength heuristics, supervised validation on the same tiny labeled set, representation-transfer metrics, or simple correlations with pretext loss alone. Without these, it is unclear whether the proposed three-factor formula adds value beyond obvious proxy signals.

Experimental details are insufficient for reproducibility. The paper does not give code, seeds, exact splits, variance across runs, implementation details for aligning pretext embeddings to target labels, or enough detail on the full SSL training protocols. Some listed torchvision parameterizations also seem ambiguous or invalid as written.

Presentation has serious issues: broken references such as “??”, duplicated text, grammatical errors, unclear notation, references appearing before appendix-like experimental sections, and figures/tables that are described mostly through captions rather than carefully analyzed. These problems make the manuscript hard to trust and build on.

The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal. The impact statement says no consequences need highlighting, and the paper does not discuss failure modes such as misleading estimates under biased labeled subsets, distribution shift, poor pseudo-label oracles, or the risk of selecting harmful pretext tasks with high confidence.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: estimating whether an unsupervised pretext task will help a downstream target task before paying the cost of full SSL training and validation.
The learnability/reliability/completeness framing is conceptually useful, and it gives a clear way to think about how a pretext task interacts with the model, data distribution, and target task.
The proposed estimator is simple and potentially useful in practice: it uses small labeled and unlabeled subsets, then combines empirically estimated indicators to predict downstream performance.

The experimental scope is a clear merit: the authors evaluate 115 augmentation-based pretext tasks across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-200, Office-31, semi-supervised and self-supervised settings, several algorithms, a second backbone, data-scale changes, and hyperparameter changes.
The ablation studies support the main design choice: combining all three indicators gives higher correlation with actual performance than using any single indicator or pair of indicators on CIFAR-10.
The cost comparison is compelling and highlights the practical appeal of the method: the estimator uses far fewer labels, unlabeled samples, and GPU time than full training and validation.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation is not fully convincing. Key events such as satisfying knowledge are not formalized precisely, Eq. 1 does not read as a standard valid probability factorization of p(y|x), and the later inequalities relating pretext-task error to target-task error are asserted rather than rigorously proved under explicit assumptions.

The empirical estimator depends heavily on a surrogate target model trained from very few labels, which is then used as a pseudo-oracle for reliability and completeness. This creates a potential circularity: the method may be measuring agreement with a weak supervised proxy rather than true downstream performance. The paper needs stronger sensitivity analysis over label counts, surrogate quality, and pseudo-label error.

The evaluation emphasizes Pearson correlation, but correlation alone does not establish accurate performance estimation or good task selection. The paper should report absolute error, rank correlation, top-k selection regret, confidence intervals, and whether the method reliably selects the best or near-best pretext task.

Some robustness results are substantially weaker than the main claim suggests, e.g. correlations around 0.453 for MoCo, 0.557 for SimCLR, 0.478 for ResNet semi-supervised, and around 0.675 on ImageNet-200. These are still positive, but they do not justify language such as accurately predicting real performance in all settings.

The benchmark consists mostly of augmentation strength sweeps. Correlations may partly arise from smooth monotonic variation within augmentation families rather than genuine generalization to qualitatively new pretext tasks. A held-out-family or cross-family evaluation would make the evidence much stronger.

Several reproducibility details are underspecified: exact thresholds for the satisfaction relation, implementation details for estimating the indicators, seed counts, variance across runs, exact train/validation splits, and code availability are unclear from the manuscript.

The presentation needs polishing. There are unresolved references such as “??”, repeated sentences, grammar issues, inconsistent terminology, and an unusual organization where appendix-like experiment sections appear after the references.

The limitations and ethics discussions are too thin. The paper should explicitly discuss failure modes, dependence on pseudo-label quality, computational assumptions, possible misuse of estimated performance in sensitive low-label settings, and cases where pretext-task selection may amplify dataset bias.
